milestones.title: count, initialise, forward
milestones.task: Write count_full, count_lora, init_adapter and lora_forward. init_adapter(d_out, d_in, r, rng) returns (A, B) using the given random.Random; lora_forward(W0, A, B, x, alpha) takes r from len(A) and returns the output vector h.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the counts for a 4096 × 4096 and an 11008 × 4096 matrix, the shapes of A and B, that B is exactly zero and A is not, that A's entries have standard deviation about 1/sqrt(d_in), two hand-computed forward passes (one at r = 1, one at r = 2 to catch a wrong scale), and on seeded random layers that the adapted layer equals the base layer at initialisation and equals (W0 + (alpha / r) B A) x once B is non-zero.
milestones.explain:
A LoRA adapter (low-rank adaptation, Hu et al., 2021) replaces the weight update ΔW of a frozen layer with the product of two thin matrices. For a layer with d_out outputs and d_in inputs, the frozen weight is W0 (d_out × d_in) and the layer computes

h = W0 x + (alpha / r) · B (A x), with A of shape r × d_in and B of shape d_out × r.

The number r is the rank of the adapter: A x squeezes the input down to r numbers, B expands them back, and the constant s = alpha / r scales the result. Two things to settle before any code.

  • Counting. The full matrix has d_out · d_in numbers. The adapter has r · (d_in + d_out): it is smaller only while r is below d_in · d_out / (d_in + d_out), which for a square matrix is half its width. The run below prints the counts for this lab's layer and for two real shapes from chapter 11 (the Llama 2 7B attention and MLP projections).
  • Initialisation. B starts at exactly zero, so B A = 0 and the adapted layer equals the pretrained layer at step 0: the first loss you see is the base model's loss, not a random perturbation's. A starts random, with entries of standard deviation 1/sqrt(d_in) so that each entry of A x is of order one. If both were zero, neither would ever receive a gradient; milestone 2 shows why.

The forward pass should go through the bottleneck: compute A x (r numbers), then B times that, never the full d_out × d_in product B A. That is what makes the adapter cheap to run on top of the frozen layer, and it is the form in which gradients are computed.

$ python3 exp_counts.py
          matrix         full  r=1                  r=2                  r=8                  r=16               
  this lab 24x24          576         48  8.33%         96 16.67%        384 66.67%        768 133.33%
  attention 4096   16,777,216      8,192  0.05%     16,384  0.10%     65,536  0.39%    131,072  0.78%
  MLP 11008x4096   45,088,768     15,104  0.03%     30,208  0.07%    120,832  0.27%    241,664  0.54%

On the real shapes, rank 16 is 0.78% of a 4096 × 4096 attention matrix and 0.54% of an MLP matrix. On this lab's 24 × 24 layer the same ranks are huge (rank 8 is two thirds of the matrix and rank 12 equals it), which is why the lab's savings are modest and its conclusions are about shape, not scale.
milestones.card:
A low-rank adapter freezes a layer's pretrained weights and learns the change as a product of two thin matrices: one squeezes the input down to r numbers (the rank), the other expands them back. The output is the frozen output plus a scaled correction.

count_full is d_out * d_in; count_lora adds the two thin matrices, A (r by d_in) and B (d_out by r). In init_adapter, B is zero, so the adapted layer starts equal to the pretrained one, while A is random with standard deviation 1/sqrt(d_in); with both zero, no gradient could flow. lora_forward scales by alpha / r (r is len(A)) and computes A x first, never the full product B A.

W0 = identity, A = [[1, 1]], B = [[2], [3]], alpha = 4, x = (1, 2)
h = x + 4 * B (A x) = (1, 2) + 4 * (6, 9) = (25, 38)

Read more: A3 chapter 11, the idea.

milestones.title: the gradients of A and B
milestones.task: Write lora_grads(A, B, x, g, alpha), which returns (dA, dB) for one sample given the output gradient g, and batch_loss_and_grads(W0, A, B, data, alpha), which runs the forward pass over a list of (x, y) pairs, returns the mean squared error and the summed gradients (loss, dA, dB). Use mse_loss and mse_grad_out from the given code.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks one hand-computed sample (dB = [[6], [-6]], dA = [[-2, -2]]), that dA is exactly zero at B = 0 while dB is not, the shapes of both gradients, and on seeded random problems with r = 3 and alpha = 6 that every entry of dA and dB agrees with a central finite difference of the loss, that the loss itself is right, and that W0 is not modified.
milestones.explain:
Training needs the derivative of the loss with respect to A and to B. Write s = alpha / r and let g = ∂L/∂h be the gradient of the loss with respect to this layer's output for one sample (a vector of length d_out; for the mean squared error, mse_grad_out gives it to you). With h = W0 x + s B A x, the chain rule from derivatives and the chain rule gives, as in chapter 11's "go deeper" box,

∂L/∂B = s · g (A x)T (d_out × r),    ∂L/∂A = s · (BT g) xT (r × d_in).

Each is an outer product. The gradient of B multiplies the output gradient by the r-dimensional bottleneck activation A x. The gradient of A first pulls the output gradient back through B and then multiplies by the input. Over a batch, the loss gradient is the sum of these matrices over samples (the 1/N of the mean is already inside mse_grad_out). Nothing here involves W0: it is frozen, so no gradient is kept for it, which is where LoRA's saving in gradient and optimiser memory comes from.

This is easy to see in the numbers. The script runs six steps of Adam on a rank-4 adapter and prints the size (Frobenius norm) of each gradient and of each matrix:

$ python3 exp_first_steps.py
step     loss      |dA|      |dB|     |A|     |B|
   0   0.3347   0.00000   0.34763   2.161  0.0000
   1   0.3156   0.05470   0.24443   2.161  0.1960
   2   0.2977   0.07062   0.14997   2.133  0.2590
   3   0.2871   0.07489   0.13119   2.113  0.3101
   4   0.2792   0.07958   0.16572   2.100  0.3495
   5   0.2678   0.08605   0.17738   2.090  0.3772

At step 0 the gradient of A is exactly 0.00000 and the gradient of B is 0.35. After one Adam step B has size 0.196 and A receives a gradient of 0.055. Note how little A moves over the first steps (its norm drifts from 2.161 to 2.090) while B grows from nothing: early on, LoRA is largely learning how to mix the random directions that A already provides. The loss falls from 0.335, the base model's loss on the noisy training set, by about 0.02 a step.
milestones.card:
Training needs the slope of the loss with respect to every entry of both thin matrices. The output depends on them through a chain, input to squeezed input to expanded output, so each gradient is an outer product: a column times a row, which makes a matrix.

g is the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer's output for one sample, which mse_grad_out supplies. Read the two products in the docstring of lora_grads like this: dB is the output gradient meeting the squeezed input; dA is the output gradient pulled back through B, then meeting the input. So while B = 0, dA is exactly zero and only dB moves. batch_loss_and_grads runs lora_forward on each pair, takes mse_loss over all of them and sums the per-sample gradients; the 1/N of the mean is already inside mse_grad_out.

A = [[1, 2]], B = [[3], [4]], x = (1, 1), g = (1, -1), s = alpha / r = 2
dB = [[6], [-6]]    dA = [[-2, -2]]

Read more: A3 chapter 11, how it trains.

milestones.title: training loops
milestones.task: Write full_grads(W, data) (returns (loss, dW)), train_lora(W0, data, r, alpha, lr, steps, seed) (returns (A, B, losses)) and train_full(W0, data, lr, steps) (returns (W, losses)), where losses[k] is the loss before step k.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks full_grads against finite differences; that LoRA at r = 1 drives a noiseless rank-1 target to almost zero loss while leaving W0 untouched, with losses[0] equal to the base model's loss and a non-zero B at the end; that the same seed gives identical training; that on a rank-2 target r = 1 plateaus well above r = 2; and that train_full recovers the target matrix without modifying its input.
milestones.explain:
With gradients in hand, training is the same loop for both methods: forward and backward over the whole training set, record the loss, take an Adam step. The given Adam class updates the matrices you hand it in place, so for LoRA the parameter list is [A, B] and the frozen W0 never goes in. For full fine-tuning the parameter is the weight matrix itself, with gradient dW = ∑ g xT over the samples. Two details matter:

  • Leave the base weights alone. train_lora must never write to W0, and train_full must work on a copy. A bug that edits the base in place makes every later comparison quietly wrong: the "forgetting" of the next run would be measured from a model that has already moved.
  • The learning rates differ. Chapter 11 reports that the best learning rate for a LoRA adapter is typically much higher than for full fine-tuning (Thinking Machines found about ten times). Here the given defaults are 0.02 for the adapter and 0.005 for the full matrix, both with full-batch Adam; with fewer parameters sharing the work, the adapter's parameters each need larger steps.

Run both on the task-B training set and watch the training loss:

$ python3 exp_curves.py
 step  LoRA train  full train
    0      0.3347      0.3347
   10      0.2342      0.2089
   25      0.1923      0.1442
   50      0.1844      0.1179
  100      0.1837      0.1101
  199      0.1837      0.1093
final clean test B:  LoRA r=2 0.0469   full 0.0871
floor if you knew W_B exactly: train loss would still be the label noise, 0.16

Full fine-tuning fits the training set better and keeps improving to 0.109, below the noise floor of 0.16 that even the true W_B would leave on noisy labels: it has started fitting the noise. The rank-2 adapter plateaus at 0.184 within about 60 steps, because it can only express a rank-2 update and the rest of the training error is label noise and the faint dense change it cannot represent. On clean held-out data the order reverses: 0.047 for the adapter against 0.087 for the full matrix. Milestone 6 turns this observation into a sweep.
milestones.card:
Fine-tuning is a loop: run the data through, measure the loss, compute gradients, let an optimiser step. LoRA trains only the two small matrices and leaves the base weights frozen; full fine-tuning trains the whole matrix. It is the same loop with different parameters.

full_grads(W, data) is the full-matrix version of the last milestone: g from mse_grad_out for each sample, and dW is the sum of g x^T. train_lora seeds random.Random, calls init_adapter, and hands [A, B] to Adam, which edits them in place. Each step it gets the loss and gradients on all the data, records the loss before stepping, then calls opt.step. train_full does the same on a copy of W0. Neither may change W0: an in-place edit quietly spoils every later comparison.

With steps=3, losses holds the losses before steps 0, 1 and 2. For LoRA the first is the untouched base model's loss, since B = 0 (0.3347 on the lab's data).

Read more: A3 chapter 11, how it trains.

milestones.title: merge and unmerge
milestones.task: Write adapter_delta(A, B, alpha) (the update matrix (alpha / r) B A), merge(W0, A, B, alpha) (a new matrix W0 plus the delta) and unmerge(W, A, B, alpha) (a new matrix W minus the delta). The helpers matmul and mat_add do the work.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks two hand-computed deltas (r = 1 and r = 2), then on seeded random layers that merge does not modify W0, that the merged layer gives the same outputs as lora_forward, that the delta has numeric rank exactly r, that unmerge(merge(W0)) returns W0, and that the delta is linear in alpha. An untrained adapter must merge to the base weights exactly, and a trained adapter on the lab's layer must merge to a layer with the same held-out loss and an update of rank 2.
milestones.explain:
After training, the adapter is a linear correction, so it can be folded into the weights: W = W0 + (alpha / r) B A, one matrix addition per adapted layer. The merged layer is an ordinary layer with no extra matrices and no extra latency, which was an explicit design goal of the LoRA paper. Three consequences are worth checking.

  • Same function. W x equals W0 x + s B (A x) for every x, up to floating-point rounding. This is only true because the adapter is linear; chapter 11 notes that merging into a quantised base rounds the sum and loses a little of the adapter's effect.
  • Bounded rank. The product B A is a 24 × 24 matrix, but it is built from r columns of B and r rows of A, so its rank is at most r. However long you train, the update never leaves a rank-r set. Full fine-tuning has no such limit.
  • Reversible. Because the merge is an addition, subtracting the same s B A recovers the base weights (up to rounding). That is what lets a service keep one base model and apply, remove and swap many adapters, the mechanism behind chapter 17's adapter libraries.
$ python3 exp_merge.py
largest output gap, adapter path vs merged matrix, over 200 inputs: 8.9e-16
rank of W0                 24
rank of merged W           24
rank of W - W0 (LoRA r=2)  2
rank of W - W0 (full)      24
largest entry error after unmerge(merge(W0)): 5.6e-17
adapter file: 96 numbers; merged layer: 576 numbers (the merged model is as big as the base)

The merged and unmerged paths agree to 9 × 10-16, the merged layer has full rank 24 (as the base does), and the update W − W0 has rank 2 for LoRA against 24 for full fine-tuning. Notice the last line: the adapter is a 96-number file, but the merged model is as big as the base. You save training memory and storage, not inference memory, unless you serve the adapter unmerged.
milestones.card:
After training, the adapter is a linear correction, so it can be added into the weights: the new matrix is the old one plus the scaled product of the two thin matrices. The merged layer is an ordinary matrix that gives the same outputs as the adapter path, and subtracting the same correction restores the original.

adapter_delta builds (alpha / r) * B A with matmul. It has the full matrix shape, but it is made from r columns of B and r rows of A, so its rank is at most r however long you train. merge returns a new matrix W0 + delta and must not edit W0. unmerge returns W - delta; mat_add(P, Q, c) computes P + c * Q, so a negative c subtracts.

W0 = identity, A = [[1, 1]], B = [[2], [3]], alpha / r = 4
delta = 4 * [[2, 2], [3, 3]] = [[8, 8], [12, 12]]; merged = [[9, 8], [12, 13]]

Read more: A3 chapter 11, merging and serving.

milestones.title: run one experiment
milestones.task: Write evaluate(W, data) (the mean squared error of the plain layer W), run_lora(world, r, ...) and run_full(world, ...). Each returns a Result: run_lora is named "LoRA r=<r>" and counts count_lora parameters, run_full is named "full" with fraction 1.0. The three losses are measured on the merged matrix over world.train_b, world.test_b and world.task_a.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks evaluate on a hand case (answer 2.0), that the base layer is near-perfect on task A and poor on task B, then that LoRA at r = 2 reports 96 parameters (fraction 0.1667), more than halves the held-out task-B loss, has a training loss above its held-out loss (the training labels are noisy) and pays a visible cost on task A; that full fine-tuning fits the training set better than rank 2; that the same call reproduces the same numbers; and that a different adapter seed changes the result a little, not a lot.
milestones.explain:
You now have everything needed to run the experiment the chapter described. A run trains a method on the task-B training set, produces a single weight matrix (for LoRA by merging), and reports one Result row with five facts: the method's name, the number of trainable parameters, that number as a fraction of the full matrix, the loss on the noisy training set, the loss on clean held-out task-B data, and the loss on task A.

The last number is the one this lab exists to produce. Fine-tuning changes the weights, the weights are shared between tasks, and nothing in the task-B loss asks the model to keep doing task A. The loss on task A is therefore a direct measure of what catastrophic forgetting (chapter 10) cost. It cannot be avoided entirely, since task B really does disagree with task A, but it can be larger or smaller depending on how much the update moves. A fair comparison needs a few rules. Both methods start from the same W0 and see the same data. Both are measured on the same merged-matrix footing, using evaluate. And the base model is the reference: it scores 0.200 on clean task-B data and 0.0002 on task A.

The ingredient to see before you write it is where the extra forgetting of full fine-tuning lives. Compare the squared size of each method's update with the true low-rank change L:

$ python3 exp_noise_fit.py
squared size ||change||_F^2 of the update each method made, and how far it is from the true low-rank change:
  true low-rank change    4.000
  true faint dense part   1.056
  LoRA r=2 update         4.093   distance to true low-rank  0.467
  full update             6.652   distance to true low-rank  2.992
  (task-A loss = ||update||_F^2 / 24 for isotropic inputs: 0.171 and 0.277)

The rank-2 adapter's update has squared size 4.09, almost exactly that of the true change (4.00) and 0.47 away from it. The full update has squared size 6.65 and is 2.99 away from the true low-rank change: on top of the real change it carries the faint dense part (1.06) and a good deal of fitted label noise, because 72 noisy samples cannot tell a real direction from a chance one. Every unit of squared size is paid for on task A at 1/24 per unit, which is 0.171 against 0.277.
milestones.card:
An experiment trains one method on the task-B data, collapses the result into one weight matrix and measures three losses: on the noisy training set, on clean held-out task-B data, and on the old task A. The last is the forgetting measure, because fine-tuning changes shared weights and nothing asks the model to keep doing task A.

evaluate(W, data) is the mean squared error of a plain matrix (use matvec and mse_loss). run_lora trains with train_lora from world.W0 on world.train_b, merges, counts parameters with count_lora and measures the merged matrix on world.train_b, world.test_b and world.task_a. run_full does the same with train_full, named "full" with fraction 1.0. Both are scored on a plain matrix, which keeps the comparison fair.

On the lab's 24 by 24 layer, rank 2 has 96 of 576 parameters (fraction 0.1667). The base model scores about 0.0002 on task A, so anything above that is damage.

Read more: A3 chapter 10, catastrophic forgetting.

milestones.title: LoRA against full fine-tuning
milestones.task: Write sweep(world, ranks, ...), which returns [full row] + [one LoRA row per rank], and verdict(rows, tolerance), which returns a dict with "smallest_rank" (an integer parsed from the row name, or None), "param_fraction" and "forgetting_saved" (1 - row.task_a / full.task_a).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks verdict on hand-built rows (including the strict-tolerance and nothing-qualifies cases), then on worlds with seeds 0 and 1: the sweep order, that rank 1 is clearly worse than rank 2 on held-out data, that rank 2 beats full fine-tuning there while rank 8 does not, that full fine-tuning fits the training set best but forgets most, that forgetting grows with rank, and that the verdict picks rank 2 with 15 to 18% of the parameters and between 20 and 50% less forgetting. It also runs the 240-sample world and checks that full fine-tuning wins and verdict returns None.
milestones.explain:
One run is an anecdote; a sweep is a result. sweep runs full fine-tuning and LoRA at several ranks on the same world, and verdict turns the table into the answer a practitioner wants: what is the smallest rank that gets close to the best result, and what does it save? Here "close to the best" means a held-out task-B loss within a tolerance (10% by default) of the best row in the table, full fine-tuning included.

The reference solution produces this for the default world (72 noisy samples). The bars show the same numbers.

Read the three columns together. Rank 1 forgets least but cannot fit task B, since the change has two independent directions and rank 1 gives it one. Rank 2 matches the structure of the change, so it gets the best held-out loss while keeping task A loss at 0.170, hardly above the 0.167 floor. Ranks 4 and 8 have spare capacity that the noise soaks up: held-out loss rises (0.053, 0.071) and so does forgetting. Full fine-tuning is the limiting case of that trend with 576 free numbers. Fewer degrees of freedom here mean less noise fitted and less forgetting; the same effect is why the LoRA literature says it "learns less and forgets less" (Biderman et al., 2024).

That is half the story. The other half is a change of regime: give each method 240 samples instead of 72.

$ python3 exp_data.py
n_train = 36: base layer test B 0.197
   full       576 params   test B 0.3000   task A 0.4851
   LoRA r=2    96 params   test B 0.0787   task A 0.1851
   LoRA r=8   384 params   test B 0.2470   task A 0.4106
n_train = 72: base layer test B 0.200
   full       576 params   test B 0.0871   task A 0.2740
   LoRA r=2    96 params   test B 0.0469   task A 0.1695
   LoRA r=8   384 params   test B 0.0713   task A 0.2395
n_train = 240: base layer test B 0.192
   full       576 params   test B 0.0177   task A 0.2195
   LoRA r=2    96 params   test B 0.0394   task A 0.1679
   LoRA r=8   384 params   test B 0.0240   task A 0.1994

At 36 samples full fine-tuning is worse than not tuning at all on the held-out data (0.300 against a base of 0.197), while rank 2 holds at 0.079. At 240 samples the order flips: full fine-tuning reaches 0.018 because it has enough data to learn the faint dense change as well, rank 2 cannot (0.039, which is close to the squared size of that dense change divided by 24, 0.044), and rank 8 closes part of the gap (0.024). Chapter 11 states this as the advice from "LoRA Without Regret" (Schulman and colleagues, 2025): LoRA matches full fine-tuning on small-to-medium datasets and falls behind when the data exceed its capacity. In this lab, capacity is literal: it is the rank. Your verdict will return a rank for the 72-sample world and None for the 240-sample world, where no rank in the sweep gets within 10% of full fine-tuning.
milestones.card:
One run is an anecdote; a sweep is a result. A practitioner wants to know the smallest adapter that gets close to the best held-out loss, and what it saves in parameters and forgetting.

sweep(world, ranks, ...) returns the full fine-tuning row first, then one LoRA row per rank in the order given, built with run_full and run_lora. verdict(rows, tolerance) takes the best test_b of any row, full fine-tuning included, and finds the first LoRA row within best * (1 + tolerance). Parse its integer rank from the row name ("LoRA r=4" gives 4). forgetting_saved is 1 - row.task_a / full.task_a. If no LoRA row gets close enough, all three values in the dict are None.

test_b: full 0.10, r=1 0.30, r=2 0.105, r=4 0.12: best 0.10, limit 0.11, so r=2
task_a: full 0.20, r=2 0.10: forgetting_saved = 1 - 0.10 / 0.20 = 0.5

Read more: A3 chapter 11, why a low-rank update can be enough.
